extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, political communicators, and policymakers studying public opinion and leadership
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze how leaders create, shape, and manage public opinion—through symbols, control of information, simplification of choices, and organized persuasion—in democratic societies. Useful for designing or evaluating political communication and mass persuasion strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and use symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders must cultivate symbols (flags, totems, slogans, revered phrases) because symbols conserve unity by focusing emotion and blurring individual differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols serve as focal points where differences merge; they discharge emotion at a common target and allow a leader to 'move a crowd.' While they can be exploited to manipulate followers, in crisis or rapid action they may be necessary to mobilize people who cannot wait for debate or full understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify mass choices into yes/no (or similarly simple) options
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass decisions require necessary simplicity—voters typically express themselves by saying Yes or No on an abbreviated ballot or a presented candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because complex reality cannot be fully presented to the mass, leaders and organizers must present concrete, simple choices that can be linked symbolically to individual opinions. Even preferential ballots depend on the quality of choices presented. Complexity of issues limits direct popular legislation's meaningfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present choices through a small, organized group
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of leaders or committees (caucus, nominating convention, steering committee) must formulate and present a definite choice to a large group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass action typically follows after a few strategically placed people define the options; successful cooperation usually requires that the Few nominate and the Many elect. Attempts to bypass this (initiative, referendum, direct primary) often only postpone or complicate the need for leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach program to existing feelings by verbal and emotional linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: When launching a program, leaders should first vocalize the prevailing feelings of the mass and then connect the new policy verbally and emotionally to those feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders identify with familiar attitudes (stories, patriotism, grievances) to gain trust, then present a plan that is associated, by analogy or symbol, with those initial feelings so the mass accepts it despite not understanding all contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control information access and frame facts selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Every official exercises some censorship over what facts the public sees; leaders choose what facts, in what setting and guise, the public is permitted to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically placing information (suppressing casualty lists, delaying totals) limits vivid public conception of harms and preserves morale or political support. Control over facts serves both to persuade the public and to protect institutions from damaging revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the incidence of policy (visibility of costs and benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders prefer policies whose burdens are remote, deferred, or dispersed, because visible, immediate costs provoke more resistance than diffuse or future costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers favor long-term debts, indirect taxation, or measures where private costs are not immediately felt; constructive policies addressing remote factors typically face less popular support than visible interventions (punishing a landlord, investigating profiteers). Evaluate policies by who directly feels the impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge effects on morale when making decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders must plan policies not only on merits but on their effect on followers' morale and willingness to perform assigned duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In military or high-risk contexts, leaders know thresholds of endurance (casualty tolerance) and may withhold candid disclosures to preserve unity. Policy decisions should account for how supporters will judge commanders or officials in light of suffering or outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scapegoats, placation and small favors to consolidate support
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'mend fences,' leaders may offer scapegoats, redress minor grievances, rearrange jobs, or placate influential factions as routine political maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine constituency service (doing small services for many rather than big public goods) and occasional visible favors are effective political strategies. Leaders target either influential individuals or blatantly uninfluential people (for spectacle) to consolidate support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture consent with organized techniques and research
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion has become a self-conscious art based on psychological research and modern communication methods; creating consent is now technical and systematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice of democratic persuasion has shifted from rule-of-thumb to analysis; knowledge of how to create consent changes political calculations. Practitioners should rely on research-based techniques rather than assume spontaneous, well-informed public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer secrecy and centralized command in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In urgent or dangerous situations, leaders may limit public debate and trust a few decision-makers to preserve unity and avoid paralysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public debate can dissolve unity and create dangerous divisions (e.g., military command during wartime); hence, secrecy and concentrated decision-making are sometimes justified to prevent immediate disaster even if wrong decisions are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of mass cognition—masses are not organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs and complex policies do not spontaneously arise in multiple minds; a mass lacks the integrative functions of a single organism and thus needs leaders to formulate policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should not assume that the public will invent synchronized programs; instead they must translate, vocalize, and organize scattered sentiments into coherent choices through leadership and symbolic linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of destructive criticism that disintegrates symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Overly analytical or candid criticism can break the transference of emotion to symbols and result in fragmentation and warring sects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders resist 'poking about' with clear definitions because it undermines the shared emotional hold of symbols. While clarity has high intellectual value, it can be politically destabilizing if it erodes the symbols holding a following together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit leaders' informational and institutional advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Established leaders have natural advantages—better information, official responsibility, control of records—and thus are more convincing and can shape access to facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional position to secure attention and speak with convincing authority; acknowledge that this asymmetric access also enables propaganda and selective presentation of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link mundane issues to larger proto-symbols to heighten stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform trivial policy questions into symbolic struggles by associating them with larger symbols (e.g., framing a subway fare as 'unAmerican').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By inserting a local issue into a national or symbolic framework, leaders mobilize stronger emotions and make small issues politically salient; this can be used to rally support or to deflect attention from substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek measured consent when publicity won't strengthen opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When publicity is unlikely to empower opposition and debate won't unduly delay action, wise leaders seek to involve subordinates to obtain some sense of free willing consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consulting subordinates and preparing them for outcomes creates the feeling of participation; this can reduce later resentment, though it inevitably contains some illusion because the full contingencies are not equally vivid to all participants.
